name: J-PAL vouchers option value CEA, 2024
summary: Helps governments that want to pilot voucher programs for health products. GiveWell's spreadsheet "J-PAL vouchers option value CEA, 2024", linked from its grant page. Every number is traced from the sheet's bottom line; calculated rows reproduce the sheet's own values.

Note, the cost value cited here ($1.19) is slightly different that in the cost-effectiveness analysis linked above ($1.21) because we've made a slight tweak to the sources we rely on for estimating programs costs since publishing that analysis. However, the overall reasoning and methodology shown in the linked analysis has not meaningfully changed.

rows.label: Portion of non-urban population reachable by program
Adjustment for some subnational areas being below CE bar for a variety of reasons (see notes section)
rows.explainer: We expect that roughly half of the areas in countries estimated to be above our cost-effectiveness bar would turn out not to meet our bar upon further investigation. This may be a result of high costs, low population density, conflict/instability in the region, or other factors.

rows.label: Adjustment for time to scale up
rows.explainer:
Rough adjustment to account for time to scale-up, i.e. if we did scale up vouchers programs it would take a long time, and so we shouldn’t count the full benefits over the full 10 year window.

The specific estimate we use (40%, i.e -60%) is a rough guess.

rows.explainer: Rough adjustment to capture a scenario where we decide to scale up a vouchers program based on information from this grant and are wrong to do so (e.g. because of bias in the pilot results).

rows.label: Risk that vouchers pilots are funded without us in a few years
rows.explainer: Rough assumption to capture the possibility that another funder might fund this program instead of GiveWell. This estimate is relatively high because J-PAL has already received some funding to deliver its program in Rwanda from a non-GiveWell funder, indicating some external interest.

rows.label: Benefit from influencing other funders/value to broader research community
rows.explainer: Rough assumption to capture benefits to the wider community from funding this work.

rows.label: Direct benefits to program participants from vouchers pilots
rows.explainer: Rough adjustment to capture benefits to participants in possible chlorine vouchers pilots, which we don't explicitly model.

rows.label: Ad hoc adjustments: Overall adjustment
Cost-effectiveness (x cash)
Units of value per dollar given to GiveDirectly
rows.explainer: GiveWell reports this model's result in multiples of cash transfers. Multiplying by GiveWell's value of a dollar to GiveDirectly converts it into units of value per dollar, so it ranks against the other models. Older sheets used older moral weights; the multiple of cash is the comparable number across years.

rows.label: Staff pay as a share of program cost
rows.explainer: Default for research, technical assistance and policy work: mostly people. Our judgment; we haven't seen this grant's breakdown.

rows.label: Pay gap versus comparable jobs elsewhere
rows.explainer: Researchers and advisers could typically earn considerably more in consulting or industry. Our judgment.

rows.label: Salary forgone by staff per dollar of cost (in-kind donation)
Share of the full cost paid in cash
rows.explainer: With credit by share of resources, staff's forgone pay counts as part of the cost, and staff get their share of the outcome. Off, this is 100%.

rows.label: Units of value per dollar
rows.explainer: With credit by share of resources, times the share of the full cost paid in cash (staff's forgone pay is the rest).
